- A single long prompt can freeze every other stream on the server: I was reading about chunked prefill, and a 24,000-token prompt admitted whole stalls decode for about 720ms (0.03ms per token), so the fix is to cap each forward pass instead of fixing the model.
  why: his own Phase 2B lesson, written 2026-09-22 and rebuilt 2026-09-23; the numbers are from his course, so it is named as reading, but the topic is exactly what he is studying this month.

args.title: Inside an LLM Server: Scheduling, Memory, and Prefix Caching
args.markdown:
Your time-to-first-token tripled this afternoon and your prompt did not change. Your client logs show the same bytes sent at the same rate. The provider returned the same answer, three times slower. Nothing on your side explains it.

The explanation is not on your side. It is inside the server, in the requests that arrived at the same second as yours. A real inference server never runs one request. It runs a loop over a batch, and your request shares a GPU with requests from strangers. This post opens that loop. Three mechanisms explain most of what you see from the outside: the scheduler, the memory allocator, and the prefix cache.

Two latency terms first. TTFT is the time to first token. TPOT is the time per output token after the first.

## 1. The scheduler loop: your latency depends on other requests

vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, and the hosted providers all run the same loop. The names differ. The steps do not.

Three more terms:

- **Prefill** is the pass that reads your whole prompt. It produces the first token.
- **Decode** is each later pass. Each decode pass produces one more token.
- A **forward pass** is one run of the model over a set of tokens.

One scheduler iteration looks like this:

```
1. look at the waiting queue and the running set
2. pick work that fits a token budget and a memory budget
3. run ONE forward pass over all of it together
4. every decoding request gets exactly ONE new token
5. finished requests leave; freed memory returns to the pool
6. go to step 1
```

Step 4 surprises most people. One iteration produces one token per request, no matter how large the batch is. A batch of 40 requests produces 40 tokens in about the time one request takes for one token.

The reason is what a decode step does. It reads all the model weights from GPU memory once, then does a small amount of arithmetic per sequence. The memory read takes most of the time. One more sequence adds only a little arithmetic. A teaching cost model makes this concrete: one decode iteration at batch size 1 takes 18.0ms, and each additional sequence in the batch adds 0.12ms. A batch of 16 then costs 18.0 + 0.12 x 16 = 19.92ms per iteration. A batch of 1 costs 18.12ms. Sixteen times the tokens for about 10% more time. The constants are a teaching model, not a measurement of any specific GPU. The shape matches real servers.

### Static batching was the old way

The old server collected N requests and ran them together. It admitted no new request until the last one in the batch finished. A request that finished early kept its slot and its GPU memory and produced nothing. The slowest request held the whole batch.

### Continuous batching is the current way

The scheduler admits new work on every iteration. A finished request leaves at once, and a waiting request takes its slot on the next step. This is called iteration-level scheduling. The Orca paper introduced it in 2022 (Yu, Jeong, Kim, Kim, Chun, OSDI 2022, usenix.org/conference/osdi22/presentation/yu).

The paper's headline number, with its conditions: FasterTransformer served 0.185 requests per second at a median normalised latency of 190ms. Orca served 6.81 requests per second, a 36.9x speedup at the same latency. The test used GPT-3 175B in fp16 on 16 A100 40GB GPUs, with input lengths drawn uniformly from 32 to 512 tokens and output lengths from 1 to 128. A note on verification: the 36.9x figure is confirmed from the paper's abstract and introduction. The detailed evaluation section was not readable in the copy I could reach, so the 0.185 req/s and 190ms conditions rest on the paper's own text and could not be independently re-checked.

A small simulator of this loop, run with 40 requests at 6 arrivals per second, gives:

| policy | mean TTFT | p99 TTFT | mean TPOT | throughput |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| static | 5,357ms | 9,215ms | 19.4ms | 2.3 req/s |
| continuous | 867ms | 2,649ms | 25.4ms | 3.6 req/s |

Three effects to read here:

- Mean TTFT fell from 5,357ms to 867ms. That is 6.2x better.
- Throughput rose from 2.3 to 3.6 requests per second. That is 57% more.
- Mean TPOT rose from 19.4ms to 25.4ms. A fuller batch decodes each token a little slower.

The third effect is not a bug. You trade a slower token for a 6x better TTFT.

The Anyscale team measured the same effect on real hardware (anyscale.com/blog/continuous-batching-llm-inference, 22 June 2023). Conditions: OPT-13B on one A100 40GB, 1,000 requests of 512 input tokens each, output lengths from an exponential distribution. Results: up to 23x throughput with continuous batching plus paged memory, up to 8x with continuous batching alone (Ray Serve and TGI), up to 4x with FasterTransformer. The 23x figure compares against simple static batching, not against a tuned server. Always quote it with that baseline.

### Why your TTFT tripled at 3pm

You do not control the provider's scheduler. You control four inputs to it: prompt length, output length, arrival pattern, and prefix reuse. The arrival pattern is the one you feel most.

Run the same simulated workload at 12 arrivals per second instead of 6. Continuous batching mean TTFT rises from 867ms to 1,674ms. Static rises from 5,357ms to 6,551ms. The prompts did not change. Only the arrival rate changed. That is the 3pm spike: more requests arrive, they wait in the queue and share the batch, so TTFT rises while TPOT barely moves.

The trap: you will try to fix a TTFT spike with retries. A retry adds one more request to the same queue. Under load, the queue gets longer and the spike gets worse.

The server-side version of the same fix now exists. vLLM v0.29.0 (released 2026-09-09) added two admission flags, --max-num-queued-reqs and --max-num-queued-tokens (pull request #49445). When the queue limit is hit, a new request is rejected with HTTP 503 instead of queueing forever. The source calls this a TTFT quality-of-service valve. The same release checks that the full prompt fits before admission (scheduler_reserve_full_isl, default True) and keeps a watermark of KV headroom to reduce preemption. The scheduling policy is still fcfs (first come first served), with priority as the only alternative. All verified from vllm/config/scheduler.py at tag v0.29.0. If you self-host, serve a 503 and let the client back off. That beats a silent queue.

Sentence to remember: **one scheduler iteration gives every running request one token. Throughput comes from batch size. Latency comes from what else is in the batch.**

## 2. The paged KV cache: why one GPU fits 18x more requests

The KV cache holds the key and value vectors of every token the model has seen. The model reads them on every decode step, so they must stay in GPU memory. How many requests fit in that memory is called concurrency, and concurrency decides how long requests wait in the queue.

Start with the simple allocator, because it shows the problem. The server admits a request but does not know how long the answer will be. So it reserves memory for the worst case: max_model_len, the longest sequence the server accepts.

For llama-3-8b in fp16, one token of KV costs 2 (K and V) x 8 KV heads x 128 head dim x 2 bytes x 32 layers = 131,072 bytes. That is 128 KB per token. Reserving 32,768 tokens per request costs 4.00 GB per request. On one 80GB GPU with a 56 GB KV pool, that admits 14 concurrent requests, with 52.9 GB of the pool sitting idle.

PagedAttention fixes this with an idea from operating system virtual memory. The KV cache of one sequence does not need one continuous region. The server splits the KV cache into fixed-size blocks, allocates a block only when the sequence needs it, and keeps a block table per sequence that maps each logical position to a physical block. Blocks need not be adjacent, and nothing is reserved for the future.

Same model, same GPU, 1,800 tokens actually held per request, 16-token blocks:

| | contiguous | paged |
|---|---|---|
| reserved per request | 32,768 tok | 1,808 tok |
| bytes per request | 4.00 GB | 0.22 GB |
| concurrent requests | 14 | 253 |
| memory actually used | 3.1 GB | 55.6 GB |
| memory wasted | 52.9 GB | 0.2 GB |

Paging admits 18.1x more concurrent requests on the same hardware. The model did not change. The GPU did not change. A request holding 1,800 tokens needs ceil(1800 / 16) = 113 blocks, which is 1,808 token slots. The 8 unused slots in the last block are the only waste paging leaves.

The PagedAttention paper measured the problem in real systems (Kwon et al., SOSP 2023, arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180). Only 20.4% to 38.2% of KV cache memory held real token state in the measured systems. Reserved slots and fragmentation took the rest. The paper splits the old waste into three kinds: reserved slots, internal fragmentation (the partial last block), and external fragmentation (free memory in pieces too small to use). Paging removes the third kind by construction, because every block is the same size, so any free block fits any request.

The vLLM authors state in their talks that paging cut waste to about 4%, and the Anyscale benchmark post repeats that figure. No written measurement method was found. Treat the exact number as the authors' claim. The same paper's section 4.5 names the scheduler rules: first-come-first-served, preemption of the latest-arrived requests first, and two recovery modes. Recovery either swaps the KV blocks to CPU RAM or recomputes them. Recompute is what vLLM's PreemptionMode.RECOMPUTE does.

### When blocks run out: preemption

The server does not return an error when the block pool empties. It preempts a running sequence: it frees that sequence's blocks and puts the request back in the queue. In recompute mode the request's prompt is prefilled again from scratch when it is re-admitted. A typical timeline: request R is decoding with 40 blocks held; a burst arrives at t=1.2s and the pool runs out; R is preempted and its blocks freed; at t=2.9s blocks free up, R is re-admitted and its prompt is prefilled again; at t=3.1s R resumes streaming. The user saw a 1.9-second pause in the middle of an answer. Your logs saw nothing, unless you record inter-token gaps.

At scale this becomes preemption-recompute thrash. If max_num_seqs admits more sequences than the KV pool can hold, running sequences get preempted, lose their progress, re-prefill, and recreate the pressure that evicted them. Throughput collapses while GPU utilisation stays high, so the dashboard looks healthy. The signature is a rising vllm:num_preemptions_total counter and a WARNING log naming PreemptionMode.RECOMPUTE. No error is raised. The fix is to lower --max-num-seqs, not to raise gpu_memory_utilization. To confirm you have this: halve concurrency and watch throughput go up. (Source: the Denpex failure encyclopedia, denpex.com/failures/vllm-preemption-recompute-thrash. It is a vendor source that gates remediation detail behind a signup. The mechanism is consistent with the v0.29.0 scheduler source and the parameter names check out, but the exact log line and counter names were not grep-checked against the source tree. Verify them on your own server.)

### The capacity knob that looks like a safety knob

gpu_memory_utilization is 0.92 by default at vLLM 0.29.0, verified in vllm/config/cache.py at that tag. (The value has drifted: it was 0.95 originally, and 0.9 by September 2023. The move to 0.92 is not pinned to a release, so any tutorial quoting 0.90 as the current default is stale.) The knob looks like a safety margin. It works as a capacity setting. Lowering it from 0.90 to 0.70 on an 80GB GPU removes 17.6 GB from the KV pool. For llama-3-8b at 1,800 tokens per request, concurrency falls from 253 to 181 requests. That is 28.5% of your capacity. There is also a byte-precise alternative: kv_cache_memory_bytes in vllm/config/cache.py at v0.29.0 sets the pool size directly in bytes and ignores gpu_memory_utilization.

The arithmetic, so you can do it before you buy hardware. Usable memory at 0.90 is 80 x 0.90 = 72GB. The weights take 16GB, so the KV pool is 56GB. One block costs 16 tokens x 128 KB = 2,048 KB. The pool holds 28,672 blocks. Each request holds 113 blocks. 28,672 / 113 = 253 requests. Weights use the same memory as the KV cache: a 70B model needs 140GB for weights alone, so it does not fit on one 80GB GPU, and each of its KV tokens costs 320 KB instead of 128 KB.

Sharing changes the number again. Two requests with the same first 1,200 tokens point at the same physical blocks. With a 1,200-token shared prefix: the prefix costs 75 blocks stored once, each request needs ceil(600 / 16) = 38 private blocks, so (28,672 - 75) / 38 = 752 concurrent requests on one GPU.

Sentence to remember: **paging reserves only the memory a request needs now, not the most it could need. That change makes high concurrency possible.**

## 3. Prefix caching inside the server: the radix tree and the eviction that ends it

The server needs a fast way to find that two prompts share a prefix. It keeps a tree keyed by the token sequence. SGLang calls its version RadixAttention. vLLM calls its version automatic prefix caching. The structure is the same: a shared system prompt hangs near the root and is stored once; each request's private history hangs below it.

The matching rule has three parts, and teams lose money on each one:

1. **Matching starts at token 0 and moves forward.** There is no match that starts in the middle. A change at position 10 ends the match for positions 10 to the end. A match cannot restart, because each block's cache key includes the hash of every earlier block.
2. **Matching happens in whole blocks.** A 1,210-token prefix under a 16-token block size shares 75 full blocks, which is 1,200 tokens. The last 10 tokens sit in a partial block and cannot be shared.
3. **Entries leave the cache.** The tree has a fixed size. When it fills, the least recently used blocks leave first (LRU). Hosted providers also remove entries after a time limit, commonly a few minutes without use.

The vLLM design document (docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/design/prefix_caching.html; the live page was rate-limited when checked, so the same document was read in the repo at tag v0.29.0, docs/design/prefix_caching.md) confirms each part in the server's own words. Each block hash is hash(parent_hash, block_tokens, extra_hashes), where the extras include LoRA adapter ids, multi-modal input hashes, and cache salts. The doc says plainly: "we only cache full blocks". Before v0.11 the hash key was not collision-free, and a collision in a multi-tenant server can expose one tenant's cached KV to another tenant. sha256 became the default at v0.11. The prefix hash is a security boundary, not just a dictionary key. There is also a cache_salt request field that salts the first block's hash, so two tenants with byte-identical prompts cannot share cached KV. One note on rule 2's future: v0.28.0 shipped partial-tail prefix reuse with matching below the physical block size (pull request #50507), though storage is still whole blocks at v0.29.0. Read the block rule as "whole blocks today, finer matching arriving", not as an eternal law.

### Measure the layout cost

A simulator of an agent loop priced two prompt layouts that hold the same information. Tokens were priced at gpt-4.1-mini's $0.40 per million input tokens, with cached tokens at 0.25x:

| layout | input tokens | cached tokens | hit rate | cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| volatile-first | 148,560 | 0 | 0.0% | $0.0594 |
| stable-first | 148,560 | 136,656 | 92.0% | $0.0184 |

Same tokens, same information, 3.22x price difference. The only change is the order of the parts of the prompt. The wrong layout puts a timestamp in the system message, so a byte near the start changes on every call and every later token is a cache miss. The failure is silent: no error, no warning, just a bill 3x higher and a worse TTFT.

This happens in production in less obvious places. One engineer running a coding agent through a Bifrost gateway and vLLM 0.28.0 measured his prefix-cached share rising from 55% to 95%, wait-for-first-word falling from 26 to 28 seconds to 7.3 seconds, and the worst wait falling from 514 seconds to 54 seconds (doug.sh/posts/vllm-kv-cache-agents, read 2026-09-19; one deployment, one model, Qwen3.8-27B on two RTX 3090s). His biggest cache-breaker was not prompt design. The mcp-go library decodes tool schemas into Go maps, Go map iteration order is randomized, and the gateway re-serialized the maps in whatever order they came out. The tool schemas sit at the top of the prompt, so one shuffle invalidated everything after them on every process start. A single workaround, tojson(sort_keys=True), moved the cached share from 78% to 95%. Fixes landed upstream as bifrost#7170 and mcp-go#984. If you build agents in Go, sort your keys before you serialize anything that goes into a prompt.

Two more facts from that incident. Block granularity is model-dependent: that hybrid linear-attention model caches in 2,048-token blocks, not 16. And the measurement recipe: hit rate is prompt_tokens_cached_total divided by prompt_tokens_total, and you find a miss cause by diffing two consecutive tokenized prompts to the first differing token, on an idle server, before you blame eviction.

### Eviction ends a good layout too

A correct layout still loses its hits when the cache fills. In the simulator, the stable-first layout hit 93.5% with no size limit, fell to 68.8% when the cache was limited to 500 blocks (5,615 evictions), and fell to 0.0% at 200 blocks. Your prompt did not change. Other conversations filled the cache. Production hit rates match: the SGLang paper (Zheng et al., NeurIPS 2024, arxiv.org/abs/2312.07104) measured 52.4% for LLaVA-Next-34B and 74.1% for Vicuna-33B on Chatbot Arena traffic, with a 50% to 99% range across its benchmarks. A hit rate near 100% comes from a synthetic test.

Sentence to remember: **the cache matches whole blocks from token 0 forward. Put what never changes first. Put what changes on every call last.**

The trap: a cache hit is never guaranteed. Do not build a cost model that assumes one. Model both the cached and the uncached price, and alert on the hit rate.

## The three pieces together

The loop decides whose token comes next. The memory decides how many requests fit. The tree decides whose prompt is free to recompute.

From the outside you see the results as mysteries: the 3pm TTFT spike, the 1.9-second pause mid-sentence, the 3x bill. From the inside each one is arithmetic you can run before it happens.

Sources: Orca (OSDI 2022, usenix.org/conference/osdi22/presentation/yu), Anyscale continuous batching benchmark (anyscale.com/blog/continuous-batching-llm-inference), PagedAttention (SOSP 2023, arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180), the vLLM prefix caching design doc at v0.29.0 (docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/design/prefix_caching.html), vLLM scheduler and cache config source at v0.29.0, SGLang (arxiv.org/abs/2312.07104), Dougal's prefix cache debugging post (doug.sh/posts/vllm-kv-cache-agents), and the Denpex failure encyclopedia (denpex.com/failures/vllm-preemption-recompute-thrash). Where a claim could not be verified against primary text, the post says so at the claim.

**What was asked.** A spine_evidence article for Inference Internals Phase 2A, with the relationship "measures": a measured comparison of chunked prefill budgets on one real server. That means numbers, hardware, a software version, and a workload.

**What the digest contains.** `quarantine/eval-thin-digest.md` holds exactly one finding: a single blog post that says chunked prefill "helps latency". The post gives no numbers, no hardware, no version, and no workload. Hunter states that nothing else was found. It is also a quarantine note, which marks it as not yet trusted as a source.

**Why I am writing nothing.** A measured comparison needs at least two measured runs with their settings. Here there are zero measurements. If I wrote the article anyway, every number on the page would be invented, and an article titled as measurement with no measurement in it is worse than no article. Rules 4 and 9 apply: write nothing, say what the note contains, and let the quiet day cost you two minutes instead of your trust.

**What would unblock this.** Hunter needs a source with an actual evaluation: the hardware (GPU model), the serving stack and version (for example vLLM with its version), the workload (prompt lengths, concurrency), and the reported numbers (TTFT, throughput, or latency at several chunked-prefill budget sizes). It must also come out of quarantine. One such article is enough for the "measures" piece; two would let me compare configurations.

One process note: I tried to load the `teaching` and `article` skills as the task asked, and neither name exists in the skill loader, so this answer is from the charter and my tutor rules alone. If those skills live under different names, tell me which and I will use them next time.
